name: pipe-and-filter
context: Sequential data transformation workflows where complex processing tasks are decomposed into independent, reusable filters connected by pipes
benefits: High reusability through compositional filter recombination
Independent horizontal scaling of individual filters
Easy unit testing with isolated filter validation
Parallel processing capability across filter stages
tradeoffs: Memory buffer requirements between pipeline stages
Bottleneck risk from slowest filter stage
Monolithic testing requirement for end-to-end pipeline
use_cases: ETL pipelines transforming data through multiple stages
Log processing with filtering, parsing, and aggregation
Stream processing with enrichment and routing
Media processing pipelines (image resize, format conversion)
Compiler toolchains (lexing, parsing, optimization, code generation)
Serverless function chaining with event-driven triggers
avoid_when: Processing steps require shared state or tight coupling
Strong transactional consistency is required across stages
Context/state overhead makes individual filters inefficient
Interactive user interfaces with bidirectional communication
Random access to data is required at multiple points
component_types: Pipe: Conduit passing data between filters (queue, channel, stream)
Filter: Processing unit with single responsibility
DataSource: Input origin (file, stream, API, event)
MessageBroker: Optional intermediate buffer for distributed部署
anti_patterns: Monolithic filter (single filter doing all processing)
Stateful filters with shared mutable state
Direct coupling between filters without pipes
Over-granular filters causing excessive serialization overhead
design_principles: Single Responsibility: Each filter performs one well-defined transformation
Statelessness: Filters should be stateless to enable parallel execution and reuse
Well-defined Interfaces: Standardized input/output schemas for filter compatibility
Idempotency: Filters should produce same output for same input (enables retry)
Encapsulation: Filters operate independently through well-defined pipe interfaces
Minimal Pipe Logic: Pipes only transport data; no routing or transformation logic
best_practices: Filter Granularity: Balance between small focused filters (flexibility) and large efficient filters (overhead)
Buffer Sizing: Large buffers reduce synchronization overhead but consume memory
Error Handling: Implement retry mechanisms and compensation transactions
State Management: If state is required, manage it externally or ensure isolation
Backpressure: Use flow control to handle varying processing speeds
Monitoring: Add metrics at each filter stage for pipeline observability
